title: My Classmates Plan for Their Careers. Why Not Their Marriages?
author: Srisha Raj
summary: A university student argues that colleges plan their students' careers in detail but treat marriage preparation as a personal side project. Her story begins at a house party where her stated five-year goal of being married with a family was dismissed as "cute". She says institutions shape culture by what they value, and that universities that promise to form whole people give advisers and internships for careers but silence on family. She cites the 2026 State of Our Unions finding that 64% of unmarried young adults call marriage an important goal, and Gallup data showing marital status predicts well-being more than a degree. On campus, she observes the "capstone model", where marriage comes after everything else, so a 22-year-old with a ring looks like she is rushing. She proposes preparing for family the way students prepare for careers, through character, finances, intentional dating and conversations in orientation and advising.
points: Campus culture rewards career planning and treats serious preparation for marriage as naive.
Most students still want marriage, and data suggest marital status predicts life satisfaction more than education does.
The capstone model keeps pushing marriage five to six years into the future, leaving dating to drift.
Preparing for marriage means character work, reflection on inherited family habits, financial literacy and dating with intention.
Her request is that universities give relationships the same dignity as professional goals in advising and orientation.
quotes: For many of us, the question isn’t whether marriage is desirable—it’s whether a lasting one is attainable. Post This

So, why isn’t preparing for marriage taken seriously on most college campuses? A major reason is that institutions shape culture by what they value—and students learn fast which ambitions earn an adviser’s support, and which ones just get a "cute.
A generation trained to plan every step of our future careers shouldn’t have to wing the commitment that matters most.
Boyfriends came and went from our halls constantly, and nobody batted an eye. Then, one of my residents got engaged.

Today, young adults' expected age of marriage sits five to six years in the future regardless of how old they are: 22-year-olds say they’ll marry around 28; 33-year-olds estimate they will marry by 39. The horizon keeps moving.

Researchers Galena Rhoades and Scott Stanley found that couples who make deliberate choices about relationship milestones, rather than sliding into them, report much higher marital quality. Deciding well is a habit built long before the big moments arrive.

That question deserves a better answer than campus silence. Writers on these pages have called for clearer guidance and preparation in dating, noting that parents, schools, and communities are leaving a major gap unfilled.
